Palladium catalyzed divergent cycloadditions
of vinylidenecyclopropane-diesters with
methyleneindolinones enabled by zwitterionic
p-propargyl palladium species †
Ben Niu, a Yin Wei b and Min Shi
 *ab
A palladium-catalyzed divergent synthesis of spirooxindoles fused
with a five- or a six-membered ring by a cycloaddition reaction of
vinylidenecyclopropane-diesters with methyleneindolinones was
disclosed. This protocol features an in situ generated unprece-
dented zwitterionic p-propargyl palladium species in cycloaddition
reactions and a switchable process between (3+2) and (4+2)
cycloadditions by changing the phosphine ligand.
Organic synthesis based on propargylic compounds has received
considerable attention and has been extensively studied due to
their versatile and specific reactivities. Consequently, palladium-
catalyzed reactions of propargylic compounds with nucleophiles
have been extremely eﬀective for the construction of carbon–
carbon and carbon–heteroatom bonds.
1 The key step in these
reactions was the formation ofZ1-(propargyl)palladium speciesB,
Z3-(propargyl)palladium species C or Z1-(allenyl)palladium spe-
cies D from the propargylic donorA in the presence of palladium
catalyst, which could undergo a variety of further transformations
with suitable cross-partners (Scheme 1).
2 On the other hand, the
regio- and chemoselectivities in the palladium-catalyzed propargyl
substitution reaction are more complicated. According to the
different reaction sites of nucleophiles and propargyl reagents,
the branched products could be alkynes,
3 allenes,4 alkenes5 and
conjugated dienes.6 The previous investigations indicated that
hard nucleophiles tended to attack the terminal or inner carbon
atom of (propargyl)palladium species to afford alkyne products E
or allene products F, while soft nucleophiles exhibited opposite
reactivity to attack the central carbon atom of (propargyl)palla-
dium species, afford ing alkene products I or conjugated diene
products J (Scheme 1). Additionally, the palladium catalyzed
annulation reactions of propargyl compounds and bis-nucleo-
philes have also been investigated.
7 The general process of
cycloaddition reactions is described in Scheme 1. The first
nucleophile attacks the central carbon atom of (propargyl)palla-
dium species to deliver intermediateK, which can be converted to
p-allyl palladium complex L upon protonation, then the second
nucleophile attacks the p-allyl palladium intermediate to provide
the cyclized products M.O b v i o u s l y ,t h ec o m p l e xr e a c t i o np r o p e r -
ties of propargyl palladium grea tly impede its application in
synthetic chemistry. Moreover, the control of regio- and chemo-
selectivity is also a difficult task for its substitution reactions. With
respect to the cyclization reaction, the substrates are restricted to
those bearing dual soft nucleophilic functional groups, leading to
a relatively single working mode. Therefore, it is quite significant
to develop novel and efficient synthetic methods to effectively
regulate regio- and chemoselectiv e cyclization reactions, subse-
quently further enriching the reaction modes based on pro-
pargylic palladium species.
Vinylidenecyclopropanes (VDCPs), which have an allene
moiety connected with a cyclopropane ring in their structural
motifs, are a class of highly strained small ring compounds,

which can easily undergo a variet y of cyclopropane ring-opening
reactions upon release of the strained ring energy. 8 As for
vinylidenecyclopropane-diesterN s h o w ni nS c h e m e2 ,i ti n c o r p o -
rated a gem-diester in the cyclopropa ne moiety. Previously, our
group and others have disclosed that a Lewis acid can eﬀectively
promote the cyclopropane ring-opening of vinylidenecyclopropane-
diesterN for a variety of interesting transformations.9 Therefore, we
envisioned that vinylidenecyclopropane-diesterN could be used as
ac o m p a t i b l ep-propargyl donor to aﬀord a zwitterionicp-propargyl
palladium intermediate (O) in the presence of palladium catalyst
with the assistance of a Lewis acid, which could act as a 1,3-(1C,3C)
or 1,4-(1C,4C)-dipole to undergo cycloadditions with interceptorP
to provide the corresponding (3+n)o r( 4 +n) cyclization productQ or
R (Scheme 2a). Herein, we wish to report our working design of the
divergent construction of spirooxindoles fused with a five- or six-
membered ring enabled by an in situ generated zwitterionic
p-propargyl palladium species (Scheme 2b).
10
Our initial examination was conducted with diethyl 2-vinyli-
denecyclopropane-1,1-dicarboxylate1a and methyl (E)-2-(1-benzyl-2-
oxoindolin-3-ylidene)acetate2a i nt h ep r e s e n c eo fP d2dba3 as a
catalyst, XantPhos as a ligand, and Yb(OTf) 3 as an Lewis acid
additive in tetrahydrofuran (THF) at 801C. Gratifyingly, the desired
(3+2) cycloaddition product3a w a so b t a i n e da sas i n g l ed i a s t e r e o -
mer, albeit in a relatively low yield of 11% (Table 1, entry 1). When
Cs
2CO3 (1.0 eq.) was used as an additive, the yield of 3a was
improved to 36% presumably because the alkaline conditions are
favorable for the formation of a zwitterionicp-propargyl palladium
species (Table 1, entry 2). Subsequently, we examined a set of
phosphine ligands and found that DPEPhos aﬀorded3a in higher
yield (42%) and rac-BINAP and XPhos failed to deliver the target
product under identical conditions (Table 1, entries 3–5). Inter-
estingly, when dppe or dppp was used as a ligand, the main product
was switched to a (4+2) cycloadduct, 4a, and the corresponding
product could be obtained in 54% (dr: 5 : 1) and 53% (dr: 7 : 1) yields,
respectively (Table 1, entries 6 and 7). Next, we employed DPEPhos

product3a was achieved in 50% yield (Table 1, entry 8). An inferior

3 (Table 1, entry 9).
Finally, we identified that by reducing the loadings of catalyst
(2.5 mol%) and ligand (7.5 mol%) as well as using degassed THF
as solvent, the corresponding product3a was obtained in 63% yield
(Table 1, entry 10, conditions A). Next, we turned our attention to
further optimize the reaction conditions for4a.W h e nt h er e a c t i o n s
w e r ec a r r i e do u ta t6 01C, the use of dppe, dppp and dppb did not
give better results (Table 1, entries 11–13). We also found that the
yield of 4a could be improved to 56% with an 11 : 1 dr by reducing
the loadings of catalyst (2.5 mol%) and ligand (7.5 mol%) as well as
performing the reaction at 80 1C( T a b l e1 ,e n t r y1 4 ,c o n d i t i o n sB)
(for more details see Schemes S1 and S2 in the ESI †). We also
investigated the stability of products3a and 4a under conditionsA
and conditionsB, respectively, and found that3a and 4a are stable
under their respective optimal conditions.
On the basis of the above optimized conditions for this
divergent cycloaddition reaction, the scope of (3+2) cycloaddi-
tion reactions between vinylidenecyclopropane-diester 1a and
methyleneindolinones 2 was first explored and the results are
shown in Scheme 3. Fixing the R
2 protecting group as a benzyl
group, the electronic eﬀects at the diﬀerent positions of the
benzene ring of isatins were investigated. We found that
regardless of whether the substituent was introduced at the
C4-position ( 2b and e ) or C5-position ( 2f), the reactions
proceeded smoothly, furnishing the desired products 3b–3f in
52–62% yields. Substrate 2g bearing 4,6-dimethyl groups at the
benzene ring of isatin was also tolerated, providing the desired
product 3g in 58% yield. Substrate 2h bearing the 4-methyl
group at the benzyl protecting group and substrate 2i having
3,5-dimethyl groups at the benzyl protecting group were also
compatible, affording the desired products 3h and 3i in 57%
and 63% yields, respectively. Then, we turned our attention
towards the different types of nitrogen-protecting groups. For
substrates 2j–2p, in which the nitrogen atom was protected

with 2-methylnaphthalene, 2-methylthiophene, methylacetate,
ethyl, isopropyl, 2-methylallyl and cinnamyl groups, the reac-
tions proceeded smoothly, giving the desired products 3j–3p in
moderate yields ranging from 42 to 58%. Under the same
reaction conditions, ( E)-1-benzyl-3-(2-oxo-2-phenylethylidene)
indolin-2-one 2q could also be converted to the corresponding
product 3q in 46% yield. However, when ( E)-1-benzyl-3-(2-oxo
propylidene)indolin-2-one 2r was employed as the substrate, a
complex product mixture was formed, presumably due to its
instability in the presence of Cs
2CO3. The structure of 3b was
unambiguously determined by X-ray diffraction, and its ORTEP
drawing is shown in Scheme 3.
Subsequently, the scope of (4+2) cycloaddition reaction was
also investigated under the optimal conditions (Scheme 4).
Substrates 2 bearing diﬀerent substituents at the C4-position
or C5-position could be converted to the corresponding pro-
ducts 4b–4d in 55–62% yields with 6 : 1–11 : 1 dr values. The
substrate bearing 4,6-dimethyl groups at the benzene ring of
isatin was also tolerated, providing the desired product 4e in
48% yield with a 6 : 1 dr. Upon replacing the benzyl protecting
group with a phenyl group, the reaction could also take place,
affording the desired product 4f in 38% yield with a 7 : 1 dr.
When the nitrogen atom was protected with different protect-
ing groups, such as 2-methylnaphthalene, 2-methylthiophene,
cinnamyl and allyl groups, the desired products 4g–4j could be
obtained in 44–53% yield with 4 : 1–9 : 1 dr values. As men-
tioned above, the corresponding product 4k could also be
acquired in 57% yield with a 7 : 1 dr when using ( E)-1-benzyl-
3-(2-oxo-2-phenylethylidene)indolin-2-one 2q as a substrate.
However, 2r was also incompatible with the optimized condi-
tions. The X-ray crystal structure of 4b is shown in Scheme 4.
The above developed optimal conditions were also applied to a
variety of vinylidenecyclopropane-diesters 1.A ss u m m a r i z e di n
Scheme 5, vinylidenecyclopropanes substituted with methyl or
iso-propyl esters could also work under both conditionsA and B,
delivering the corresponding products 3r and 3s and 4l and 4m
(dr: 7 : 1–8 : 1) in moderate yields. WhenN-propyl was introduced
at the terminal allene moiety of1, the (4+2) cycloaddition product
4n was obtained in 47% yield with a 3 : 1 dr under conditions B,
but a complex mixture was p roduced under conditions A.
A plausible mechanism for the (3+2) and (4+2) cycloaddi-
tions is depicted in Scheme 6. The catalytic cycle was initiated
by the Pd– p-propargyl species I, formed from Pd(0) and 1a with
the assistance of Lewis acid Yb(OTf)
3. The nucleophilic carbon
anion of intermediate I attacked 2a to afford intermediate II.
On one hand, by using DPEPhos having a large bite angle as a
ligand,
11 the carbon anion selectively attacked the inner carbon
atom to afford the (3+2) cycloaddition product 3a via its
resonance structure III or IV (path a). On the other hand, using
dppp having a small bite angle as a ligand, the carbon anion
selectively attacked the Pd– p-propargyl unit at its central car-
bon atom to generate the corresponding pallada-cyclobutene
intermediate V, which could produce the p-allyl palladium
species VI upon protonation. The subsequent base-induced
b-hydride
12 elimination would regenerate the palladium(0)
catalyst and produce the corresponding product 4a (path b).
A more detailed mechanistic investigation will be carried out in
due course.

The catalytic asymmetric version of this divergent cycloaddi-
tion was also investigated (see Table S1 in the ESI † for more
details) and we found that using L1 as a chiral phosphine
ligand could deliver 3a in 33% yield along with 31% ee
(Scheme 7a). Finally, a scale-up synthesis was performed with
5.0 mmol of substrate 1a and 2.5 mmol of substrate 2a under
both conditions A and B, aﬀording the corresponding products
3a and 4a in 52% and 47% (dr: 7 : 1) yields, respectively
(Scheme 7b).
In summary, we have disclose da ne ﬃ c i e n ta n dc o n v e n i e n t
synthetic protocol to produce spirooxindoles fused with a five or
six-membered ring by the reaction of vinylidenecyclopropane-
diesters with methyleneindolinones in the presence of palladium
catalyst and a Lewis acid. By simply switching the ligands, an
unprecedented zwitterionicp-propargyl palladium catalyzed regio-
divergent cyclization is realized to enable (3+2) and (4+2) cycload-
ditions. This discovery sheds light on the development of
propargyl palladium species rel ated reactions and enriches the
diversity of its reaction mode. F urther investigations on the
asymmetric version of this palladium-catalyzed divergent cycload-
dition and application of this protocol to the synthesis of biolo-
gically active substances are underway.
